So:

Radioland Murders - it's a comedy about a string of murders that happen in a radio station during a live broadcast. It's set in the '30s. It's well written and well acted, but more than anything else, it's a tremendous bit of editing. It shifts back and forth between the events that are happening in the studio and the stuff that's being broadcast, and it all comes together into one seamless experience.

Night on Earth - actually, I'd suggest pretty much any Jim Jarmusch movie. They're all worth seeing. Night on Earth is the most fascinating one to me though. It's actually five separate vignettes, set in five different cities around the world (LA, New York, Paris, Rome and Helsinki) and all five stories actually all happen simultaneously. But since they're at different points on the globe, they're actually happening at various times of the night, from early evening in LA to early morning in Helsinki. And they're told in that order, so the effect is to span one night. And the mood of each story fits that theme, from cautious optimism in the evening in LA through increasing craziness as the "night" progresses, to a somber and weary finale as the sun rises in Helsinki. And, as a bonus, the Rome vignette, starring Roberto Benigni, is simply one of the funniest things I've ever seen.

Jabberwocky - this is actually Terry Gilliam's first non-Python movie (though it starts Michael Palin anyway). It's a sort of retelling of the story of the Jabberwocky, but since it's Gilliam, it's mostly silly yet perceptive social and political satire.
